Create
kree-AYT
v.
Latin creare, to bring forth, produce, beget. In the KJV it renders Hebrew bara, a verb whose subject in the Old Testament is never anyone but God—a grammatical fact that carries a doctrine.

Biblical Definition

In Scripture, to create is what God does and what no creature does. The Hebrew bara is used some fifty times, and in every one God is the subject; men build, form, make, fashion and beget, but they do not create. The Bible opens with it: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1)—no pre-existing material named, no assistant credited. It is used again at the summit of the sixth day, three times in one verse for emphasis: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them (Gen 1:27). Man's nature, his image-bearing, and his being made male and female are all inside the creating act, which is why they are not his to renegotiate. Isaiah presses the point against every rival: I have made the earth, and created man upon it: I, even my hands, have stretched out the heavens (Isa 45:12), in a passage that mocks the clay for arguing with the potter. The New Testament assigns the work to Christ: by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth... all things were created by him, and for him (Col 1:16). And the verb reappears in salvation, which Scripture treats as a second creation of the same order: we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works (Eph 2:10). A man cannot create himself the first time or the second.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CREATE as to produce; to bring into being from nothing; to cause to exist—and secondarily to make or form by investing with a new character, as to create a peer.

expand to see more

CREATE, v.t. — To produce; to bring into being from nothing; to cause to exist. In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1).

CREATE, v.t. — To make or form, by investing with a new character; as, to create a peer. Also, to produce; to cause; to be the occasion of; as, to create confidence.

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:1 — "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."

Genesis 1:27 — "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."

Colossians 1:16 — "For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:"

Ephesians 2:10 — "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them."

Modern Corruption

The verb has been handed to the creature: men now speak of creating themselves, their truth, their gender and their reality—taking the one word Scripture reserves for God alone and making it the banner of self-definition.

expand to see more

Ordinary usage has diluted create until it means little more than make—creating a document, a playlist, content. That drift is harmless enough. The serious corruption is ontological: the claim that a person creates himself. Create your own truth, create your identity, create the life you want. Scripture's grammar forecloses it before the argument starts, because bara never takes a human subject. Men are creatures the whole way down. What God made in the creating act—image-bearing, and male and female—is given, and the clay does not get a vote on the potter's work.

The distinction to keep is the one the older language kept: God creates, man makes. Human making is real, dignified, and commanded—cultivate the garden, build the ark, weave the curtains, write the psalm. It is the image-bearer doing in miniature what his Maker does infinitely, but always with material already given. When a culture forgets that difference it does not become more creative; it becomes unable to receive anything, since everything must now be self-authored. And it has no answer for Ephesians 2:10, where even the new self is created in Christ Jesus by someone else's hand.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bara, to create, whose subject is always God; Greek ktizō, to create or found—the verb of Colossians 1:16 and Ephesians 2:10.

expand to see more

Hebrew bara (H1254) — to create, shape, bring into being; used with God as subject only, never of human making (Gen 1:1, 21, 27; Isa 43:1; 45:12).

Hebrew asah (H6213) — to make, do, fashion from existing material; the verb men share with God (Gen 1:7; Exod 25:8).

Greek ktizō (G2936) — to create, found, bring into existence; used of the first creation and of the new man in Christ (Mark 13:19; Eph 2:10; Col 1:16; Rev 4:11).

Usage

"In the beginning God created—no material named, no assistant credited."

"Genesis 1:27 puts the image and male-and-female inside the creating act."

"God creates; man makes. The clay does not vote on the potter's work."
